e.meaning: grace, as a Breton-style form of Anna
e.etymology: From French Anaelle, which arose in Brittany as Anna, grace, with the -aelle ending of Gaelle; it is also taken as the feminine of the angel name Anael. Popular in France since the 1990s.
A spelling of Yiddish Liba, from lib, dear or beloved. In the US it is used mostly in Orthodox and Hasidic Jewish families.
From Sanskrit varnika, a word related to varna, color, that is used of fine or pure gold.
A feminine form of Hebrew Aviel, God is my father, also heard as Ava with the -ella ending of Gabriella and Isabella.
A French spelling of Abigail, from Hebrew Avigayil, my father's joy. In the Bible Abigail is the wise woman who becomes a wife of King David.
A surname, in some families a shortened form of the Irish name McCovey. Covey is also the English word for a small flock of quail or partridges.

e.meaning: one who lives by a spring or well
e.etymology: An English surname for someone who lived by a well or spring, from Old English wella.
From the Mul Mantar, the opening verse of the Sikh scripture, which describes God as nirvair, without hatred: nir, without, and vair, enmity.
A spelling of Darren, a 20th-century name of unclear origin, possibly from an Irish surname. This is the spelling used for Darrin Stephens, the husband on the 1960s TV comedy Bewitched.

e.meaning: pet form of Candace; also the word for sweets
e.etymology: A pet form of Candace or Candice, from Kandake, the title of the queens of ancient Kush. The match with the word for sweets gave it much of its 1960s appeal.

assoc.t: candy, the everyday word for sweets

e.note: Identical to the word for sweets, so jokes about it are likely.

e.etymology: An English place name and surname: the farm or settlement of a man named Ceadda, the Old English name that became Chad.

assoc.t: Chadwick Boseman, star of Black Panther

e.etymology: From Hebrew yamin, right hand, a sign of strength and favor. In the Bible Jamin is a son of Simeon; the same word forms the second half of Benjamin.
An older Italian and Spanish form of Jerome, from Greek Hieronymos, sacred name. It is best known as the name Mexicans gave the Apache leader Goyahkla.

assoc.t: Geronimo!, the shout made when jumping

e.etymology: From Arabic walid, newborn, from the verb walada, to give birth. Two Umayyad caliphs bore the name as al-Walid.
A Latin American spelling of Johnny, the pet form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. The Jh- order is common in Colombia, Venezuela and Peru.
From Old Norse Einarr, from elements meaning one or alone and warrior. It shares its root with the einherjar, the fallen fighters of Valhalla.
A modern American name that reshapes Taylor with the -on ending of Jaylon and Daylon.
From Swahili neema, grace or bounty, borrowed from Arabic ni'ma, blessing.
A biblical Hebrew name, borne by the eldest son of Levi. It is related to Gershom and usually derived from garash, to drive out: an exile or sojourner.
A modern name built on the English word allure, attraction or charm, which comes from Old French. Princess Allura is the heroine of the Voltron animated series.

assoc.t: Princess Allura of the Voltron cartoons

e.etymology: From the Quran, where Tasnim is a spring of paradise whose water is the drink of those nearest to God.
A spelling of Amir, from Arabic amir, commander or prince, the source of the title emir.
A form of Anna, Hebrew for grace, on the model of Ania and Anya. Annia was also the feminine of the Roman family name Annius, borne by women of the imperial family.
A spelling of Nayla or Naila, from Arabic na'ila, one who attains what she seeks. It also fits the American pattern of Kayla, Layla and Nyla.
A spelling of Tidus, the hero of the video game Final Fantasy X, written to give the TYE-dus pronunciation. It also resembles Tydeus, a warrior of Greek myth.
The South Asian spelling of Arabic Hudhayfah, the name of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, a trusted companion of the Prophet Muhammad.
The English animal word, from Latin leo and Greek leon, used directly as a name in place of Leo, Leon or Lionel.
A respelling of Axton, an English surname and place name taken up as a first name in the 2010s beside Axel, Paxton and Jaxton.
A recent one-syllable coinage on the pattern of Bryce and Jace, with the Ky- of Kyle and Kyson.
A clipped form of Emiliano, the Spanish and Italian form of Latin Aemilianus, from the Roman family name Aemilius, traditionally linked to aemulus, rival.
From Slavic kaziti, to destroy, and mir, peace or world: a warrior's name. Several rulers of Poland bore it as Kazimierz, and Saint Casimir is a patron of Poland and Lithuania.
